meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Few people think more than two or three times a year; I have made an international reputation for myself by thinking once or twice a week'?
meta.ogDescription: Shaw quip or 1933 magazine filler? The earliest known appearance is an unsourced Reader's Digest 'Quotable Quotes' item; no Shaw work contains it.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1856–1950 · Irish playwright, critic and polemicist; Nobel Prize in Literature, 1925
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Shaw and entirely in keeping with his public wit, but no play, preface, letter or interview of his has been found containing it. The earliest known appearance is an unsourced filler item in The Reader’s Digest for May 1933, which says only that Shaw “once addressed a company” — no date, no audience, no citation — and Quote Investigator ↗ could not determine where the magazine got it.

source.heading: The trail stops at a 1933 magazine filler

docMeta.dd: May 1933, volume 23, quote page 16 (verified on microfilm by Quote Investigator)

source.excerpt: George Bernard Shaw once addressed a company as follows: “I suppose that you seldom think. Few people think more than two or three times a year. I have made an international reputation for myself by thinking once or twice a week.”
trail: The earliest instance known to Quote Investigator ↗ is an item in the “Quotable Quotes” department of The Reader’s Digest for May 1933, page 16, verified on microfilm. It supplies no date, no audience and no citation.

It travelled by reprint rather than by witness, and it was being trimmed as it went: Commercial West on 6 May 1933 and the Hartford Courant on 1 October 1933 carried the Reader’s Digest text exactly, while the Christian Science Monitor ran a slightly briefer form on 25 August 1933 — dropping the opening sentence — which the Chester Times reprinted on 13 September 1933, all catalogued by QI ↗.

Searching Shaw’s own remarks about mental exertion, QI found only a letter of 14 December 1894 to the young journalist Golding Bright about the frequency of writing — “you must write, write, write every day for several years…” — which it calls only tangentially related to the quotation being explored. Read the investigation ↗
The line appears nowhere on Wikiquote’s George Bernard Shaw page ↗ — not among the sourced quotations arranged by work, and not in its Attributed, Disputed or Misattributed sections.
source.excerptNote: The complete item as it ran in the “Quotable Quotes” department, transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from microfilm. Note the opening sentence — already being dropped by reprints in August 1933, and gone from the version shared today — and the full stop where the internet now puts a semicolon.

source.rightsNote: The wording has never been tied to a work by Shaw, so there is no publication whose date could settle its copyright status; the earliest known carrier is an anonymous item in a 1933 magazine, which is itself after the pre-1931 line for automatic US public domain. Quotle asserts no rights status for this line — treat it as unresolved rather than free to reuse.

author.name: George Bernard Shaw
author.heading: About George Bernard Shaw
author.metaLine: 1856–1950 · Irish playwright, critic and polemicist · Nobel Prize in Literature, 1925
author.bio: Shaw was an Irish playwright, critic, polemicist and political activist, born in Dublin on 26 July 1856 and dead in Hertfordshire on 2 November 1950. His plays — Pygmalion, Major Barbara, Saint Joan, Man and Superman — are among the most performed in English, and he received the Nobel Prize in Literature for 1925. He was also, by the 1930s, one of the most quotable public names alive; that fame is exactly why quips he cannot be shown to have said still travel under his byline, this line among them.

No source in Shaw’s own works has been identified.

misattribution.heading: How the attribution actually works
misattribution.intro: Nobody has proposed a rival author for this line. The problem is narrower and more common: Shaw’s name was attached to it by a magazine that never said where it got it, and everything since has copied that magazine.

items.scope: Presented as a sourced Shaw quotation
items.who: Goodreads, BrainyQuote, AZQuotes and the rest of the quote web
items.why: Goodreads ↗ carries the exact semicolon wording credited to Shaw with no book, speech or date attached, and notes on the same page that its quotations are added by the community and not verified. That is the standard presentation across the quote sites.

The earliest text is three sentences separated by full stops and opens with “I suppose that you seldom think,” which the Christian Science Monitor had already dropped by August 1933 and which the modern version lacks too; a 1963 newspaper columnist trimmed it further by removing “for myself”, per Quote Investigator ↗.

This is the earliest known appearance of the remark. QI ↗ notes that the magazine solicited and paid for reader-contributed quotations, that its vetting process is unknown, and that QI cannot say where this one came from.

misattribution.truthLine: Honest answer: Shaw may well have said something like this from a platform, but nobody has produced the occasion, the transcript or a text of his containing it — the documented record begins with an unsourced magazine item in May 1933 ↗.

context.heading: Why a line like this sticks to Shaw
lead: By 1933 Shaw was one of the most quoted men alive: a Nobel laureate since 1925, a dramatist of international fame, and a standing fixture of newspaper humour columns. That is exactly the condition in which a sourceless one-liner attaches itself to a name — a magazine prints a witty sentence, credits Shaw, and every reprint afterwards cites the reprint rather than an occasion.

The spread is visible in the record. The item ran in the financial trade publication Commercial West on 6 May 1933 and in the Hartford Courant on 1 October 1933, both matching the magazine word for word; the Christian Science Monitor printed a slightly briefer form on 25 August 1933 under the heading “Shaw Thinks”, losing the opening sentence, and the Chester Times reprinted that shortened version on 13 September 1933 — all documented by Quote Investigator ↗, and not one of them a witness to Shaw saying it.
context.detailsSummary: What the 1933 text actually said — and how it changed
detailsBody: The earliest text is three sentences, not two. It opens with “I suppose that you seldom think,” a sentence the Christian Science Monitor had already cut by August 1933 and which the modern version omits entirely, and it separates the two surviving sentences with a full stop rather than the semicolon now standard online.

The semicolon form that circulates today matches the text Quote Investigator quotes from a 1949 New York Times review of Evan Esar’s The Dictionary of Humorous Quotations, where Shaw appears as a dictionary entry with the line printed beneath his name — still with no source attached. A Baton Rouge columnist in 1963 trimmed it again, dropping “for myself”. See the citation trail ↗
context.pull: “QI does not know where the magazine obtained the quotation.” — Quote Investigator
